tasks.spec: You are designing a model of how time is negotiated in a conversation, not fixing a bug. BOUNDARY: read only inside your own task directory; everything is staged in ./source/. Never modify anything outside your task directory, never call an API, never send a message. You own exactly one output file: ./report.md. THE SITUATION: an SMS agent books eye exams. Its handling of WHEN a patient wants to come has been extended case by case over many hours, and every new phrasing has produced another patch. The owner's diagnosis is that this is solving individual situations instead of architecting the logic, and he is right. Your job is the model itself. READ ./source/TEMPORAL-BRIEF.md FIRST AND COMPLETELY. It lists every temporal thing a real patient has said in testing and what currently happens to each, the measured accepted and rejected forms of the scheduler, the measured platform limits, and the current design. Every measurement was executed against the live system; treat them as fixed, you cannot take new ones, and a design contradicting them is worthless. Also read ./source/v54_graph.json, the current live graph, and ./source/build_v54.py which generates it. THE CENTRAL DIFFICULTY: a patient's sense of time has direction (earlier, later), relativity (than what you just said, than the week we were discussing), exclusion (not Friday), open-endedness (any day as long as it is after 4), and memory (same time as last time). The current design holds a single day window plus one part-of-day word. Meanwhile the platform gives you no counter, no variable-indexed extraction, no compound routing conditions, no way to compare two variables, and a model that has failed three times when asked to carry more than one closed-class token across a boundary. DELIVER, in this order: (1) a representation of temporal intent, saying exactly what it holds, what it deliberately cannot hold, and what the model must produce per turn given the one-token constraint; (2) a resolution rule turning that into scheduler queries given the accepted and rejected forms, the ignored time parameters and the 14-day cap, including what happens when one request needs several queries and how many is too many; (3) a navigation model for later, earlier, a different day, the latest, the earliest, and a judgement on whether fixed-offset paging is the right primitive at all; (4) a single consistent rule for what the patient is told when their request cannot be served exactly, covering partially matched, out of range, unparseable and empty; (5) where each decision lives, model versus routing condition versus gateway dependency. OUTPUT CONTRACT for ./report.md: start with '# Temporal Negotiation Model'. Include '## Summary' with at most 3 bullets, then '## Findings', then '## Clean', then '## Assumptions'. Each finding uses exactly: '### Finding: <one line>' then 'Evidence:' citing a node id, a measured form or a captured variable, 'Impact:' in terms of what a patient experiences, 'Fix:' concrete enough to implement, 'Priority: P0|P1|P2|P3', 'Confidence: high|medium|low'. Cite real node ids from the graph. Then '## The Model' setting out the representation, the resolution rule and the navigation model. Then '## Node Shape' describing the graph that implements it, naming what each node decides and what it is forbidden from deciding. Then '## Migration' ordering the changes so the system is never left worse than it is now. Then '## Not Fixed By This'. HARD RULES: never invent a node id, a platform capability or a scheduler form; the brief states what exists. Do not propose prompt-tightening as a primary fix, several rounds are already documented as insufficient. Do not design something that only works if the ignored time parameters get fixed, unless you also give the interim shape. If you conclude the requirement cannot be met on this platform, say so plainly and say what you would do instead. Under 2500 words.
tasks.verified: report.md has all required sections plus the model, node shape and migration, cites at least 6 real node ids, invents none, and every finding carries evidence, impact, fix, priority and confidence

tasks.spec: You are designing a complete tool surface so a conversational agent can reach every capability of a booking gateway, rather than the handful of hardcoded webhook nodes it uses today. BOUNDARY: read only inside your own task directory; everything is staged in ./source/. Never modify anything outside your task directory, never call an API. You own exactly one output file: ./report.md. CONTEXT: an SMS agent books eye exams for an optometry practice through a gateway that fronts the practice management system. Today the agent has a small number of hand-built webhook nodes covering patient lookup, availability, conflict check and booking. The owner wants a proper tool surface: something that can reach EVERY endpoint, read EVERY field a response returns, and supply EVERY field a request legitimately accepts. READ ./source/mott-aws-webhooks.json FIRST: it is the operation catalog, with 18 operations, each carrying an id, aliases, purpose, status, effect, path, body template, upstream variables with meaning and safe source, response data with JSONPaths, and routing pathways. Also read ./source/mott-aws-gateway-reviewed-state.json for which endpoints are actually live and which are blocked or legacy, ./source/TEMPORAL-BRIEF.md for the measured behaviour and platform limits, and ./source/v54_graph.json for how webhook nodes are shaped today. YOUR JOB: (1) Inventory what a complete surface would cover: every operation, split by effect into read and write, flagging any the reviewed state says is not live. (2) Decide the right granularity: one tool per endpoint, one per intent, or a smaller number of parameterised tools, and defend the choice against the measured platform limits. Note in particular that a request body is a fixed template in the graph, that an unfilled variable becomes a JSON null the gateway rejects, and that routing compares one variable to one string literal with no AND. (3) Specify, for each tool, its inputs with which are required, its outputs with the JSONPath each is read from, what a failure looks like and how it is detected, and which routing conditions a caller needs. (4) State the safety boundary explicitly: which tools may be called without a human in the loop, which may write, and what must be true before a write. Writes today go only through one governed signing route. (5) Say what a caller must NEVER be allowed to supply, given that a model composing a payload value has already caused a patient to be booked at a time they were never offered. OUTPUT CONTRACT for ./report.md: start with '# Gateway Tool Surface'. Include '## Summary' with at most 3 bullets, then '## Findings', then '## Clean', then '## Assumptions'. Each finding uses exactly: '### Finding: <one line>' then 'Evidence:' citing an operation id, a JSONPath or a node id, 'Impact:', 'Fix:', 'Priority: P0|P1|P2|P3', 'Confidence: high|medium|low'. Cite real node ids from the graph. Then '## Tool Catalog' listing every tool with inputs, outputs, failure detection and safety class. Then '## Not Exposed' listing what you deliberately leave out and why. HARD RULES: never invent an endpoint, a field or a JSONPath; the catalog is the source of truth for what exists. Do not expose a write path that lets a caller supply a time or a patient identifier that did not come from a prior gateway response. Under 2200 words.
tasks.verified: report.md has all sections plus a tool catalog with inputs, outputs, failure detection and safety class per tool, cites at least 5 real node ids, invents no endpoints or fields

tasks.spec: You are building a complete field inventory for a booking gateway, so that nothing it can return or accept is left unreachable. BOUNDARY: read only inside your own task directory; everything is staged in ./source/. Never modify anything outside your task directory, never call an API. You own exactly one output file: ./report.md. READ ./source/mott-aws-webhooks.json, the operation catalog: 18 operations, each with an id, path, body template, upstream variables and response data with JSONPaths. Also read ./source/mott-aws-gateway-reviewed-state.json for which endpoints are live, blocked or legacy and for the response contract, ./source/v54_graph.json for which fields the live conversation graph actually reads today, and ./source/TEMPORAL-BRIEF.md for measured response shapes. YOUR JOB: produce two tables. FIRST, every REQUEST field across all operations: the field name, which operations accept it, whether it is required, what it means, and whether the live graph currently supplies it. SECOND, every RESPONSE field across all operations: the JSONPath, which operation returns it, what it means, and whether the live graph currently reads it. Then identify the gaps that matter: response fields that exist and are never read, request fields that exist and are never supplied, and any field the catalog documents that the reviewed state contradicts. For each gap say what capability is lost by leaving it unused, so the owner can judge which are worth wiring up. Pay particular attention to fields that would remove a known workaround: the graph currently reads slot list positions 0, 1, 8, 9, 16 and 17 because time filtering is ignored, and formats times as raw strings because no human-readable field exists. OUTPUT CONTRACT for ./report.md: start with '# Gateway Field Inventory'. Include '## Summary' with at most 3 bullets, then '## Findings', then '## Clean', then '## Assumptions'. Each finding uses exactly: '### Finding: <one line>' then 'Evidence:' citing an operation id or JSONPath, 'Impact:', 'Fix:', 'Priority: P0|P1|P2|P3', 'Confidence: high|medium|low'. Cite real node ids from the graph where relevant. Include the two tables in full. HARD RULES: never invent a field, a JSONPath or an operation id. Where the catalog and the reviewed state disagree, report the disagreement rather than picking one. Under 2000 words.
tasks.verified: report.md has all sections plus both field tables, cites at least 5 real node ids, invents no fields or operation ids
